projects.name: World Wide Lens
projects.subtitle: A world news wire set as a newspaper — four desks, two outlets, one filing per item
projects.description: A front page over live RSS: The Guardian and BBC News, filed to four desks and printed as each outlet wrote it — headline, standfirst, opening paragraphs, its own photograph and credit, and a link back. No accounts, no feed, no commentary.
projects.role: Solo — interface, wire parser, typographic system, deployment

sections.overview:
World Wide Lens is a world news wire laid out as a newspaper. Four desks — World, Climate, Economy,
Europe — carry everything two outlets filed, newest first. One item is one filing: the headline, the
standfirst, the opening paragraphs, the photograph the outlet filed with it and its credit, the time it
was filed, and a link back to the full text.

There is no account, no favourites, no infinite feed and no ranking. The only editorial act is which
filing gets the top of the page and which gets a small card.
sections.problem:
The first version was a NewsAPI demo: a list of articles with a search box, which is what every news
aggregator already is. The interesting question was not how to fetch more articles but how to make a
screen of news that behaves like a printed page — fixed hierarchy, a dateline, a credit line, columns,
and an end.

Two constraints came with that. A personal project has to read the wire from somewhere free, with no
key and no quota. And a printed page has to survive the wire being short: most of what an RSS feed
carries is a headline and one sentence, not an article.
sections.solution:
`data/wire.ts` reads eight RSS feeds — The Guardian and BBC News, four desks each — and maps every item
into one `Story` shape. Guardian's `<description>` carries the article's opening paragraphs as escaped
HTML, so those filings arrive with a body and take the front page and the desk rails. BBC's carry one
sentence, so they arrive as briefs and take the **In brief** rail. The layout sorts them without being
told to.

The look is one stylesheet, `styles/editorial.css`, of CSS custom properties: an ink scale, a type
scale, rules, folio apparatus and motion timings. Every component is Tailwind utilities reading those
tokens. No colour is used anywhere — a hover changes ink density, never hue.

`data/stories.ts` is a fixture: twelve invented filings with CC-licensed photographs. It is what the
screens render when a feed cannot be read, so the layout never comes back empty, and it is labelled as
placeholder copy wherever it appears.
sections.features:
- Live wire from eight RSS feeds, no API key, cached 15 minutes server-side
- Two outlets, two shapes: filings with paragraphs go to the front page, one-liners go to In brief
- The lead is chosen, not hardcoded — the longest filing among the twelve newest on the world desk
- A filing that lands in two of its own feeds prints once, on the first desk it reaches
- Each item carries the photograph its outlet filed with it, in grayscale, with the credit under it
- The plate is capped at the width the outlet filed, so it is never scaled up
- Four desks with a running head that keeps the desk vocabulary on screen while the columns scroll
- Search over the whole wire with the query as the page's headline and matched terms inverted as ink
- Search suggestions derived from the topics the wire actually filed most, not a fixed list
- Filing pages set as a page: headline full width, plate left, standfirst and source block in the
  margin with the related filings, then the text across the whole measure in three columns
- A brief says it is a brief instead of repeating its standfirst as if it were an article
- Live UTC dateline, issue number, colophon — and everything printed in monochrome
- The fixture keeps the screens rendering when a feed is unreachable
sections.architecture:
Next.js 14 App Router, all screens server components except the clock, the nameplate and the desk nav. `getWire()` fetches the eight feeds in parallel with `next: { revalidate: 900 }`, dedupes by slug, sorts by publish time and returns `{ stories, lead, front, briefs }`. Search, related filings and the desk split are pure functions over that list, so they run identically on the live wire and on the fixture. The parser is regex over the item blocks rather than an XML library: `decode` un-escapes entities and CDATA, `paragraphs` splits the description on `

` blocks when the outlet escaped them and falls back to the whole string when it did not, and `imageOf` takes the largest picture the item offers. BBC's image host serves any width under `/standard//`, so its 240-wide thumbnail is asked at 768; Guardian signs every width, so the largest one in the item is taken and its height is read from the crop box the host names in the URL. Two self-checks run without a network: `data/stories.check.ts` guards the fixture and the column counts the front grid is written against, `data/wire.check.ts` parses two real feed items captured off the wire and asserts both come out as the same `Story`.
sections.challenges:
The wire is messier than a demo. Guardian files the same story into two of its own feeds, so the front page printed it twice until items were deduped by slug — 280 items became 236. Guardian's `` holds escaped `

` tags while BBC's holds plain text, so the paragraph splitter has to handle both without an XML parser. Guardian's image URLs carry `&` inside them and are signed per width, so the largest variant has to be selected from the item rather than requested. Three layout defects were found by measuring twelve live filings rather than by looking at one: - `figcaption` was the second cell of the same grid row as the image, so the credit printed **beside** the photograph on 12 of 12 pages. - `.photo { width: 100% }` in a 792px column rendered a 700px picture at 792px — a 1.13× upscale, on 12 of 12. The plate is now capped at the width the outlet filed. - `.ink:hover` re-assigns `--fg-soft` from `--ink-2`, which the dark-mode block never inverted, so on a dark page the standfirst and the folio line went to `#18181b` on `#09090b` — 1.12:1, i.e. the text vanished on hover. Grid rows were also the quiet problem: a row is as tall as its tallest card, so a card with two lines of standfirst was stretched to the height of one with eight, and the filing page's margin column came up hundreds of pixels shorter than the plate beside it. Both now carry content down to the same line.
sections.future:
Filings from different outlets that describe the same event are still printed as two separate items —
clustering them into one event with its differing leads is the next real feature. Desk pages print every
item the desk received, which at 53 filings makes a 13,000px column; the desk needs a page count. The
old NewsAPI layer is still in the repository and wired to nothing. The two image hosts the wire asks for
should replace the wildcard in `next.config.mjs`.

projects.name: GamersLobby
projects.subtitle: A storefront over the IGDB game catalogue, with search, favourites and a playtime log
projects.description: A React and Express storefront over the IGDB game catalogue: search any of its 388,273 titles, keep favourites on the account and log the hours played per title.
projects.role: Solo — interface, backend routes, session, deployment

sections.overview:
GamersLobby is a store view over IGDB's game catalogue. Three screens carry it: a Store with a featured
carousel and genre rails, Search game with a filter bar and a grid or list view, and a profile that
holds the titles you hearted and the hours you logged. The Store shows the shelf IGDB's members rated
most; a typed title is searched at IGDB itself, so all 388,273 records are reachable, not only the
thousand on the shelf.

Everything on screen comes from IGDB: the list, the per-title description, the screenshots and both
scores. IGDB publishes no price and no player count, so the interface shows neither — the numeral on
a card is the score its members gave.
sections.problem:
The first version was a MERN demo that showed a list of games and nothing you could do with them.
The interesting parts were missing: a session that survives a reload, favourites that live on the
account instead of in the page, and a way to keep track of what you actually played.

The catalogue also has to come from somewhere a personal project may use for free, and the client
secret for that source cannot live in the browser.
sections.solution:
The frontend is Create React App with TypeScript and Tailwind, and one hand-written stylesheet
(`src/styles/arcade.css`) that carries the whole look through `arc-*` classes and CSS custom
properties — colour ramp, type scale, spacing, radii, durations and breakpoints are tokens, not
per-component decisions.

The backend is Express with Mongoose: `/register`, `/login`, `/user/:id`, `/userUpdate`, `/favorite`
and `/rmfavorite`. Login answers with a JWT and an httpOnly cookie; the page keeps the token in
`localStorage` and decodes it to restore the session, because the cookie cannot be read back from
JavaScript.

Playtime is stored per browser under a key namespaced by the signed-in user id. The user record has
no playtime column yet, so this is a deliberate local store rather than a fake server field.
sections.features:
- Featured carousel with keyboard arrows, dots, auto-advance, and a reduced-motion path; the three it features are not repeated in the rails below
- The navigation bar floats off the page edges, and its one underline slides from the tab you were on to the one you picked
- Debounced search sent to IGDB's own full-text index, so a title outside the loaded shelf is found
- Filter bar with genre chips derived from the fetched catalogue, plus newest / oldest / A–Z sorting
- Grid and list views over the same filtered result
- Every card is the same shape: a 3:4 cover shown whole, two title lines, a fixed-height genre strip
- Favourites saved on the account and restored after a reload
- Hours logged per title with `+1 h` and `+5 h` buttons
- The title page is two columns: the trailers and every screenshot on the left, a card on the right with the cover, the short description, the release date, the developer and the publisher
- The title page waits for the media and shows a shimmering skeleton until the screenshots and trailers arrive
- Arrow keys move the media carousel, both on the plate and inside the full-size view
- Favourites and the hours log require a signed-in account; a visitor gets the way in instead of controls that would silently do nothing
- Related titles come from IGDB's own `similar_games` list and from a query for the same developer's other games
- The opened image fills 90% of the viewport and closes on an outside click, Escape or its own button
- The screen lives in the URL hash, so the browser's back and forward work and each screen starts at its top
- The whole card opens a title; the heart sits in a higher layer and keeps its own click
- Profile editor with gamertag and bio validation
sections.architecture:
`frontend/` builds to a static bundle on Vercel. `backend/` is TypeScript compiled with `tsc` and run
by Node on Render. IGDB authenticates with a Twitch application token: the backend asks
`id.twitch.tv/oauth2/token` once, caches the token in memory for its ~56-day life, and refetches it
if IGDB answers 401.

`GET /api/games` runs two Apalypse queries against `api.igdb.com/v4/games` and returns them as
`{ popular, latestReleases }`, which the frontend de-duplicates by id into one list.
`GET /api/search?q=` sends one `search` query to the same endpoint and returns up to 100 matches.
`GET /api/game/:id` adds the long description, the critic score, the media — the cover, every
screenshot and the trailers, which IGDB carries as YouTube ids, each with a strip thumbnail and a
1920-wide plate version — and the two related lists, IGDB's `similar_games` expanded into full cards
plus a second query for the same developer's other titles. The plain `GET /games/:id` endpoint does not
expand those relations, so this goes through the query endpoint. IGDB's `artworks` array is not asked
for: it holds key art, wallpapers, box art and the title's logo in one list, separated only by an
`image_type` reference.

Locally the frontend calls `/api/games` relative and CRA's dev proxy forwards it, because the
deployed API's CORS allowlist answers only to `gamerslobby.vercel.app`.

`GET /health` exists so the free Render instance can be kept awake: a free web service spins down
after 15 minutes without inbound traffic, and the next visitor pays about a minute of wake. The
service asks its own public `/health` every four minutes.
sections.challenges:
IGDB has no popularity feed and no free-to-play flag, and a query caps at 500 rows, so the shelf is
built from what its members actually rated: the 500 titles with the most ratings, plus the 500 released
in the last 400 days that carry at least one. Sorting by the mean score alone instead surfaces obscure
titles sitting on two perfect votes. The first cut filtered the shelf to PC, which hid Grand Theft Auto
VI — IGDB catalogues it as Xbox Series X|S and PlayStation 5 only — so the platform filter is gone and
every card shows the platforms the entry really has. IGDB also carries entries dated 2030 to 2040, so
the recent rail needs a ceiling at today's date. A search for one title returns its deluxe edition, its
Game-of-the-Year pack and its add-on mode as separate games: IGDB's own `category` field is empty on
all 388,273 records and `version_parent` covers only 8,120 of them, so the duplicates are collapsed by
comparing the returned titles against each other instead of trusting a flag. Card art is 3:4 because the
covers are: 986 of the 1,000 rows on the shelf carry a 3:4 cover and none a 16:9 one, and IGDB's image host
answers only its named presets — a request for an arbitrary crop (`c_fill,h_450,w_800`) comes back 404 — so a
wide card cannot be cut from a cover. 81 of those same 100 titles do carry a 16:9 screenshot, which is the
only dynamic route to a 16:9 card and would widen the shelf request from 157 KB to 267 KB per 100 titles.

On the interface side the fixes were mostly measurement: a rail that overflowed its column instead of
scrolling, a focus ring clipped by the rail's own overflow box, a profile header whose content was
taller than its padding box, a featured panel that changed shape per slide because its release date
wrapped only for some titles, and a featured plate that resized per slide (548 → 614 → 519 px at 1280)
until the panel was given one fixed height and its genre row a fixed box — 720 × 420 px on every slide
now. Ordering the catalogue by
newest instead of by member votes also put one-vote releases on the front page, so the shelf keeps the
order its members rated and Newest stays a sort you pick. The deployed API kept answering with the old
catalogue after the switch because Render's build command was only `npm install` while the start command
ran `node build/index.js` — a compiled `build/` folder carried in the repository and in Render's cache,
never rebuilt from `src/`. The build command now runs `tsc` and the compiled output is no longer committed.
sections.future:
Playtime moves to the user record when the backend gains the column. The JWT is signed but not
verified on the account routes — that is the known gap, and it is the first thing to close before
this is anything other than a personal project. IGDB allows 4 requests per second, so a real cache
of the catalogue on the backend is the next thing worth building.

projects.name: WeVibe
projects.subtitle: A landscape-photo feed where the sessions and the threads hold
projects.description: A social platform for landscape photography built end to end — feed, likes, two-level threaded replies, profiles, JWT sessions and image uploads kept out of the records.
projects.role: Solo — data model, auth, interface, deployment

sections.overview:
A feed of landscape photography with the parts a feed needs to be more than a list: accounts that
survive a reload, comments that nest under other comments, likes that persist, and uploads that stay
out of the database row.
sections.problem:
The versions I kept finding stopped at the feed. The interesting work — a reply that belongs to a
comment rather than to a post, a session that lasts, an image stored somewhere other than the
document that references it — was the part nobody showed done properly.
sections.solution:
Posts, comments and replies are separate Mongoose collections with parent references, so one thread
renders from a single query instead of a chain of them. Sessions are JWTs signed with `jose`;
passwords are hashed with bcrypt; the verification mail goes through Nodemailer. Images upload to
ImageKit and the document keeps only the URL. Reads go through server components, mutations through
server actions, and every mutation route re-reads the session from the cookie rather than trusting
what the client sent.
sections.features:
- Infinite feed in batches of eight, with a shuffled deck that does not repeat what is on screen
- Likes, and comments with one level of replies under them
- Profiles with posts, a with-media tab, followers and following lists
- Meet people: every account ordered by followers, each one followable in place
- Search by username, profile editing, email and password change, account deletion behind a
  password confirmation
- Verified badges granted by the site, never chosen by the account
- Loading states that show the shape of what is arriving instead of a button that changes its mind
sections.architecture:
Next.js app router on Vercel, MongoDB (Atlas) with Mongoose documents for users, posts, comments and
replies. Public catalogue pages use time-based revalidation so repeat visits do not touch the
database. The interface is one stylesheet of design tokens plus Tailwind utilities, with a bottom
tab bar under 640px and a left rail above it. Sessions are cookies: fourteen days with Remember me,
one hour without.
sections.challenges:
The first thread model needed one query per comment and fell over on long threads; replies moved
into their own collection. Feed paging flickered because the scroll observer was rebuilt on every
loading flip and re-fired for a strip already on screen — the guard now lives in a ref, and the
observer is rebuilt only when the tab changes. Controls that depend on who is signed in pulse while
the session is being read, so a Follow button never paints on your own profile and flips a beat
later.
sections.results:
Live on Vercel with a working feed, likes, threaded replies, editable profiles and account deletion.
Built and maintained by one person across the data model, the auth, the upload pipeline and the
interface.
sections.future:
Two levels of reply is a deliberate limit; deeper nesting is not planned until there is a reason for
it.
